terminal.description: A shell in your workspace. Build Ambrose's quotes here and run them, after you call your functions from main.

tasks.title: Fold two functions into one template
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 1` in `src/quotes.cpp`, write a function template called `largestOf`, with one type `T`, that takes a reference to a `const std::vector<T>` and gives back the largest of its items, as a `T`. The vector always holds at least one item. A type `T` needs to offer only two things for `largestOf` to work: it can be copied, and two of its values can be compared with `<`. Once it works, delete `largestTicket` and `largestBill` above it, and use `largestOf` in `main`.

Check calls `largestOf` from code of its own with lists of whole numbers, prices and texts, once with `T` said in angle brackets, and with a type of its own that can be copied and compared with `<` and offers nothing else. It reads what comes back and its type.
nextSteps: Read `largestTicket` and `largestBill` side by side: only the type differs.
Write the template line, then the function once more with `T` wherever the type was.
Use only `<` between two items, and start from an item of the list.
Call it in `main` with `tickets` and with `bills`, and build.
hints: The two functions above Task 1 are one recipe written twice. A template is that recipe written once, with a name for the type that changes.

Every `int` or `double` in the recipe becomes `T`: the vector it takes, the variable that keeps the largest and what it gives back. Check's own type cannot be made from a number and has no `>`, so the largest starts from the first item and only `<` compares.
The shape is `template <typename T>` on the line above `T largestOf(const std::vector<T>& items) {`, then the body of `largestBill` with `T` in place of `double`.

tasks.title: Keep a value between two others, for any type
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 2`, write a function template called `clampTo`, with one type `T`, that takes three references to a `const T`: a value, a low end and a high end. It gives back `low` when the value is below `low`, `high` when the value is above `high`, and the value itself otherwise, as a `T`. As in Task 1, a type `T` needs to offer only copies and `<`.

Check calls `clampTo` with whole numbers, prices and texts, once with `T` said as `double`, and with its own type that offers only copies and `<`. It reads what comes back and its type.
nextSteps: Write the template line, then the first line: three `const T&` in, a `T` back.
Ask whether the value is below the low end first.
Then ask whether the high end is below the value, written with `<`.
Try it in `main` with a price and with a text.
hints: One `T` for all three values means the compiler works out one type from all three, and they must agree.
"The value is above high" is the same question as "high is below the value", and that one is written with `<`, the only comparison Check's own type has.
The shape is `if (value < low) { return low; } if (high < value) { return high; } return value;` under `template <typename T> T clampTo(const T& value, const T& low, const T& high)`.

tasks.title: Keep the quotes between the floor and the ceiling
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 3`, write a function called `fairPrices` that takes the quotes as a reference to a `const std::vector<int>`, the floor as a `double` and the ceiling as a `double`. It gives back a new `std::vector<double>` with one price for each quote, in the same order: the quote kept between the floor and the ceiling by `clampTo`, worked out as a `double`, so the pence of the floor and the ceiling are kept.

Check builds this task with a `clampTo` of its own in place of yours, written as Task 2 asks, that counts its calls and notes the type `T` it was called with. It calls `fairPrices` with quotes, floors and ceilings of its own, an empty list included.
nextSteps: Write the first line: a `const std::vector<int>&` and two `double`s in, a `std::vector<double>` back.
Go through the quotes, and keep each between the floor and the ceiling with `clampTo`.
Build it, and read the error for the line that calls `clampTo`.
Push each price onto the vector you give back, and print them from `main`.
hints: A quote is an `int`, and the floor and the ceiling are `double`s. `clampTo` has one `T` for all three.
The compiler never picks between two types for one `T` by itself: you say which type `T` is, or you hand it three values of one type. The lesson shows both.
The shape is `prices.push_back(clampTo<double>(quote, floor, ceiling));` inside a loop over the quotes.
